n: Job begins his longest reply yet (chapters 12–14), answering all three friends.

f.g: Job’s response closes the first round of speeches.

n: He opens with sarcasm: Surely you are the only people who matter, and wisdom will die when you do!

f.g: Biting sarcasm at their know-it-all attitude.

n: I understand as much as you do. Everyone knows the things you’ve said — they’re common knowledge, not special insight.

f.w: I am not inferior to you

n: Job has become a joke to his friends — a righteous man who once prayed and was answered, now laughed at.
Those who are comfortable look down on people who are slipping. It’s easy to scorn trouble when you’re not in it.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean “contempt for misfortune” — the comfortable look down on the struggling.

n: Meanwhile robbers’ homes thrive, and those who provoke God live securely. Job points out that real life doesn’t fit the friends’ neat theory.
Ask the animals and birds — they will teach you.

f.g: Nature itself shows that God controls all things, good and hard.

n: Ask the earth and the fish of the sea — they will tell you too.
All creation knows the Lord’s hand has done this. Interestingly, this is the only place in Job’s dialogues where the personal name “the LORD” (Jehovah) is used.

f.w: the hand of the LORD hath wrought this

f.g: Jehovah (YHWH) — used only here in the poetic dialogues of chapters 3–37.

n: Every living creature’s life and every human breath is in God’s hand.
Just as the tongue tastes food, the ear tests words. Job will judge his friends’ arguments for himself.

f.w: Doth not the ear try words?

n: Wisdom is supposed to come with age, they say. Job may be quoting their own claim — Bildad appealed to the elders (Job 8:8).

f.g: Possibly a quoted proverb that Job goes on to challenge.

n: But true wisdom and power belong to God. Job now begins his own hymn to God’s power (verses 13–25).

f.w: With him is wisdom and strength

n: What God tears down cannot be rebuilt; whom He imprisons cannot be freed.
He holds back rain and there is drought; He sends water and there are floods.
Power and wisdom are His; both the deceiver and the deceived are under His control. Nothing is outside His reach.

f.w: the deceived and the deceiver are his
f.g: Both the one led astray and the one who misleads are under God’s rule.

n: God strips advisers of their power and makes judges look foolish. The rest of this hymn shows God humbling the proud.

f.g: Stripped, barefoot — led away as captives.

n: He removes the authority of kings and binds them like prisoners.

f.w: girdeth their loins with a girdle
f.g: Ties a rope around them like captives.

n: He leads priests or princes away stripped and overthrows the powerful.
He silences trusted advisers and takes away the judgment of elders — undercutting the friends’ appeal to the wisdom of the aged.
He pours contempt on nobles and weakens the strong.

f.w: weakeneth the strength of the mighty
f.g: Literally “loosens the belt of the strong.”

n: He brings hidden things out of darkness into the light. Nothing is hidden from God.

f.w: He discovereth deep things out of darkness

n: He makes nations great and then destroys them, expands them and then scatters them. History is in His hands.

f.g: Narrows, confines — or leads away into exile.

n: He takes away the sense of the world’s leaders and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland.

f.w: a wilderness where there is no way

n: They grope in the dark and stagger like drunkards. Job agrees God is all-powerful — his question is not whether God rules, but why He allows the righteous to suffer.
